title: What Exactly Are We Going Back To?
author: Andrew Marcinek
summary: Andrew Marcinek addresses the growing parent movement to pull screens out of schools, epitomized by Schools Beyond Screens and the circulation of Jared Cooney Horvath's The Digital Delusion at board meetings, by asking what exactly an analog return is supposed to restore. He contrasts two uses of the same technology from his own life: the TV cart that filled forty minutes with passive watching when he was a student, and the pilot episode of Lost he used as a high school English teacher to have students trace allusions to Lord of the Flies. The argument is that purpose, lesson design, and the thinking demanded of students matter far more than the medium or a minute count, and that worksheets and packets can waste instructional time just as effectively as apps. Marcinek concedes what the early 1:1 era got wrong, putting the device before instructional design, and cites the digital use divide and PISA correlations showing moderate device use associated with higher scores than none or heavy use. His constructive move is a 'default off' habit and a five-pillar Recalibration Framework that asks the same questions of every tool and worksheet, ending with a challenge to leaders to explain in one sentence why any screen is in front of a child.
points: A minute cap treats twenty minutes of building something the same as twenty minutes of watching something and says nothing about the busywork packet that fills the time once lids close.
Marcinek argues the early 1:1 rollouts failed by handing over hardware with little training, so the device simply became 'the new cart' and the packet moved into the learning management system.
'Default off' reframes 1:1 as guaranteed access when learning calls for a device, with the lesson beginning from the teacher, question, or text and technology added only if it contributes something.

The Recalibration Framework's five pillars (Purpose Before Platform, Active Over Passive, Teacher First Tech Second, Audit Plan and Report, Communicate the Why) are meant to be applied to worksheets and products alike, not just screens.
He redirects parents from asking 'How many minutes?' to asking what their child was doing, what they were thinking about, and why it required a device.
quotes: Nobody called that screen time, but that’s exactly what it was. It was time that got filled instead of used, with a screen or a sheet of paper standing in for teaching, and it was a regular part of school long before anyone unboxed a Chromebook.

But the word “back” is carrying a lot of weight in that argument. Back to what? I went to the analog school. It had passive watching. It had busywork. Do we really think the teacher who parks a class on an app for forty minutes becomes a different teacher when the app turns into a packet?

We put the device before the instructional design. We handed over the hardware, offered little training, and in too many rooms the device turned into the new cart. The video moved from the television to the Chromebook and the packet moved from the copier to the learning management system.
A 1:1 program should guarantee every student access to a device when the learning calls for one. It should never mean the device is open all day. The default position is closed.

A cap treats twenty minutes of building something the same as twenty minutes of watching something, and it has nothing to say about the packet that fills the time once the lids close. Under a minute count, my Lost lesson and movie day are the same forty minutes. They weren’t. Restriction without instruction is incomplete policy, and that’s true whether the thing being restricted is a phone, a Chromebook, or a television on a cart.

The pressure this fall is to prove you’re listening by taking something away. Resist that reflex, and resist the opposite urge to defend everything you bought. Make closed the default position of the device.
But pressure alone is not an instructional strategy, and neither is swapping a Chromebook for a notebook.
